title: Implicit and Explicit Conversions
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of implicit and explicit conversions in C#.
Choose an appropriate type for a simple application scenario.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: A conversion changes a value from one type to another. C# permits certain implicit conversions when they are safe for the language's conversion rules, while explicit conversions require a cast or conversion operation and may lose information or fail.
understand.whyItMatters: Conversions connect data from different sources and prevent accidental data loss when values move between numeric types.
understand.analogy: A conversion is like transferring a measurement between units, where some directions preserve the value and others may round or lose detail.
understand.analogyLimit: C# conversions are governed by type rules, not a universal measurement system; some explicit conversions can overflow or throw in checked contexts.

explain.narrative:
## Implicit conversions

An implicit conversion is permitted by the compiler without a cast. For example, an int can be converted to long because every int value is representable by long. A numeric conversion may still change precision in some type combinations, so understand the language rules.

## Explicit conversions

A cast such as (int)someDouble makes a conversion explicit. Converting a floating-point value to an integral type truncates the fractional part toward zero. Narrowing integral conversions can lose high-order bits or throw in a checked context.

## Checked conversions

Use checked when an overflow should be reported rather than silently following unchecked conversion behavior. A cast does not mean that the original value is guaranteed to fit.

## Baseline

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.

examples.explanation: Every int value fits in long, so the compiler permits this implicit conversion.

examples.title: Explicit numeric cast
examples.explanation: The cast converts double to int by truncating the fractional part toward zero.

examples.title: Convert an int to double
examples.explanation: The conversion from int to double is implicit because the target type can represent the integer value.

examples.title: Use checked narrowing
examples.explanation: The value is stored in a variable before the checked conversion. The conversion therefore runs at runtime, detects that 300 is outside the byte range (0–255), and throws OverflowException, which the catch block handles.

examples.title: Convert a character to its code unit
examples.explanation: A char-to-int conversion is implicit and yields the UTF-16 code unit value.

questions.prompt: Which conversion normally requires no cast from int to long?
questions.explanation: The compiler permits int-to-long as an implicit numeric conversion.
Converting a floating-point value to an integral type truncates the fractional part toward zero.

questions.prompt: Why use checked for a narrowing conversion?
options: To convert the value to text
questions.explanation: checked causes an overflow exception when the conversion result is outside the target integral type's range.

questions.prompt: Which operator expresses an explicit cast?
questions.explanation: A cast expression names the target type in parentheses before the value.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of narrowing a numeric conversion?
questions.answer: Information can be lost or overflow can occur
options: Information can be lost or overflow can occur
The value always becomes more precise
The variable becomes a reference type
The program automatically rounds to the nearest integer
questions.explanation: Narrowing conversions can discard information or overflow depending on the types and context.
